Key Concepts

saving result in R

packages
install.packages("dplyr")
library(dplyr)


Data frames and dplyr
Main verbs: - filter() — choose rows based on conditions. - select() — choose columns. - mutate() — add or modify computed columns. - arrange() — sort rows; use desc() for descending order. - group_by() + summarize() — calculate statistics by group, similar to SQL aggregation.


Pipelines
new_data <- counties |>
  filter(moe_pct > 10) |>
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) |>
  select(name, moe_pct)


Getting ACS data
library(tidycensus)

data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c("VARIABLE_ID_1", "VARIABLE_ID_2"),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2014,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)


GEOIDs
Treat GEOIDs as strings, not numbers, so leading zeros are preserved. Typical components: - State: 2 digits - County: 3 digits - Census tract: 6 digits - Block group: 1 additional digit when applicable A state + county + tract GEOID is usually 11 digits.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
[Your 200–250 word reflection goes here.]
Among California counties, Alpine and Sierra have the greatest relative uncertainty in their median age estimates. Alpine County has an estimated median age of 41.1 years and a margin of error (MoE) of 4.8 years (11.68% of the estimate). Sierra County has an estimated median age of 56 years and a MoE of 5 years (8.93%). Both are measured less precisely than other counties.
Using relative MOE cutoffs of 0.5% and 1%, the 16 high-confidence counties average roughly 1,711,758 residents, compared with 25,185 for the 16 low-confidence counties. The 26 moderate-confidence counties average 440,450. This pattern reflects how the ACS works: it surveys a sample of residents, and smaller counties yield fewer observations, so their estimates carry more uncertainty.
Suppose a state agency used median age to prioritize funding for older-adult services. An underestimated median age might cause a county to miss support; an overestimate might divert funding from communities that need it. Alpine and Sierra would be especially exposed to such errors. Agencies should weigh MoE alongside point estimates — and recognize that median age alone does not capture the number of older residents who need services.

Optional challenges - For those craving more
Using 2023 ACS five-year estimates, I compared the precision of median age estimates for Los Angeles County and its census tracts. The county’s relative MOE was 0.26%, while the median relative MOE across 2,477 valid tracts was 10.12%. Another 21 tracts were excluded for missing estimates.
With reliability thresholds at 5% and 10%, 181 tracts (7.31%) fell into high confidence, 1,037 (41.87%) into moderate, and 1,259 (50.83%) into low confidence.
A precise county estimate does not guarantee equally precise estimates at the tract level. Smaller areas yield fewer survey observations and more uncertainty. Agencies directing older-adult services to specific neighborhoods should check tract-level MOEs rather than relying on county precision alone.

text:
Key Concepts

Anscombe’s Quartet
The four datasets have the same or nearly identical mean x, mean y, correlation, and regression line, but very different distributions when plotted.


How to Build a ggplot

Step 1: Assign an object and create a blank canvas
p <- ggplot(data)

# You can also start without specifying data
p <- ggplot()


Step 2: Define aesthetic mappings
aes() maps data to visual properties such as position and color.

Inside aes(): map a variable or category to a visual property.
Outside aes(): set a visual property to a fixed value.

# Map the category "blue" to color.
# This creates a legend labeled "blue";
# it does not necessarily make the points blue.
ggplot(county_data) +
  aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct, color = "blue") +
  geom_point()

# Set all points to blue
ggplot(county_data) +
  aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")

# Color points according to the city variable
ggplot(df, aes(x = income, y = rent)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = city))


Step 3: Choose a geometry



Function
Purpose




geom_histogram()
Show the distribution of a variable


geom_point()
Show the relationship between two variables


geom_boxplot()
Compare distributions across groups


geom_col()
Compare values across groups


geom_line()
Show changes over time


geom_errorbar()
Display uncertainty



p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = income, y = rent, color = city)) +
  geom_point()
The + operator adds layers or other plot components.



ACS Error and Reliability

Standard Error (SE)
For an ACS margin of error reported at the 90% confidence level:
\[
SE = \frac{MOE}{1.645}
\]


Coefficient of Variation (CV)
\[
CV = \frac{SE}{\text{Estimate}} \times 100%
\]
CV thresholds from the class notes:



CV Level
Range
Interpretation




Low
< 15%
High reliability


Medium
15%–30%



High
> 30%
High sampling error





Uncertainty in Derived Estimates
When calculating sums, proportions, or ratios, account for uncertainty in the original estimates. Both the numerator and denominator may have sampling error.








Function
Purpose
Example




moe_sum()
Calculate the MOE of a sum
Add populations across several areas


moe_prop()
Calculate the MOE of a part-to-whole proportion
Population in poverty ÷ population for whom poverty status is determined


moe_ratio()
Calculate the MOE of a general ratio
Number of jobs ÷ number of housing units





Changes Over Time
When comparing ACS multiyear estimates, use periods with non-overlapping years.
Convert each period’s MOE to its standard error:
\[
SE_1 = \frac{MOE_1}{1.645},
\qquad
SE_2 = \frac{MOE_2}{1.645}
\]
Assuming the two estimates are independent, the standard error of the difference is:
\[
SE_{\text{diff}} = \sqrt{SE_1^2 + SE_2^2}
\]
Define the difference as:
\[
\text{Difference} = \text{Estimate}_1 - \text{Estimate}_2
\]
The Z-score is:
\[
Z = \frac{\text{Estimate}_1 - \text{Estimate}2}{SE{\text{diff}}}
\]
The 90% confidence interval for the change is:
\[
\text{Difference} \pm 1.645 \times SE_{\text{diff}}
\]

title: Verify the Claim: Did Philadelphia’s Poverty Rate Change Significantly?
text:
Read the origin report.
I examine whether poverty rates in Philadelphia changed significantly between the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS five-year periods. I use census tract estimates from Census Bureau Table B17001, “Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age.” Specifically, I use the population for whom poverty status is determined (B17001_001) as the denominator and the population below the poverty level (B17001_002) as the numerator. The two periods do not overlap.
The following hypothesis is made:
\(\text{H}_0\): The poverty rate in tracts of Philadelphia is not changed from 2010 to 2017.


Show code
library(tidycensus)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(gt)

# H0: The poverty rate in tracts of Philadelphia is not changed from 2010 to 2017.

acs_list <- c("B17001_001", "B17001_002")

format_poverty <- function(df){
  df %>%
  mutate(
    variable = recode(
      variable,
      "B17001_001" = "Total Population",
      "B17001_002" = "Population in Poverty"
    )
  )%>%
    pivot_wider(
      id_cols = c(GEOID, NAME),
      names_from = variable,
      values_from = c(estimate, moe),
      names_glue = "{variable}_{.value}",
      names_vary = "slowest"
    )
}

poverty_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = acs_list,
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2010,
  survey = "acs5"
) %>%
  format_poverty()

poverty_2017 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = acs_list,
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2017,
  survey = "acs5"
) %>%
  format_poverty()

Code
The following code provide info for later discussion.


Show code
poverty <- poverty_2010 %>%
  inner_join(
    poverty_2017,
    by = c("GEOID", "NAME"),
    suffix = c("_2010", "_2017")
  )


poverty_withrate <- poverty %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate_2010 =
      `Population in Poverty_estimate_2010` /
      na_if(`Total Population_estimate_2010`, 0),

    poverty_rate_moe_2010 = tidycensus::moe_prop(
      num = `Population in Poverty_estimate_2010`,
      denom = na_if(`Total Population_estimate_2010`, 0),
      moe_num = `Population in Poverty_moe_2010`,
      moe_denom = `Total Population_moe_2010`
    ),

    poverty_rate_2017 =
      `Population in Poverty_estimate_2017` /
      na_if(`Total Population_estimate_2017`, 0),

    poverty_rate_moe_2017 = tidycensus::moe_prop(
      num = `Population in Poverty_estimate_2017`,
      denom = na_if(`Total Population_estimate_2017`, 0),
      moe_num = `Population in Poverty_moe_2017`,
      moe_denom = `Total Population_moe_2017`
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    cv_2010 = poverty_rate_moe_2010 / 1.645 / poverty_rate_2010 * 100,
    cv_2017 = poverty_rate_moe_2017 / 1.645 / poverty_rate_2017 * 100
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    delta_p = poverty_rate_2017 - poverty_rate_2010,
    delta_moe = sqrt(poverty_rate_moe_2010^2 + poverty_rate_moe_2017^2)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    max_p = delta_p + delta_moe,
    min_p = delta_p - delta_moe,
    include_zero = ifelse(min_p <= 0 & max_p >= 0, TRUE, FALSE)
  )

Findings
Of the 376 testable census tracts, 36 showed statistically significant increases in poverty rates and 27 showed significant decreases at the 90% confidence level. title: Week 4: Go Spatial!
text:
Key Concepts

table join

inner_join(): Keep matching records only.
left_join(): Keep all left-table records; unmatched values become NA.
full_join(): Keep all records from both tables.



Spatial Data and CRS

get_acs(..., geometry = TRUE): Return census data with spatial geometry.
Sticky geometry: Geometry stays attached during table operations; remove with st_drop_geometry().
CRS: Defines how coordinates represent locations.
Geographic CRS: Longitude and latitude, measured in degrees.
Projected CRS: Planar coordinates, usually measured in meters or feet.
NAD83: Common datum for North American data.
WGS84: Global datum used by GPS.



Map Projections

Types: Cylindrical, conic, and planar/azimuthal.
Conformal: Preserves local angles and shapes.
Equal-area: Preserves area.
Equidistant: Preserves distances along specific lines or from specific points.
Azimuthal: Preserves directions from a central point.
UTM: Uses 60 zones and meter-based coordinates, normally positive within the appropriate zone.



Essential sf Functions







Function
Key purpose




st_crs(x)
Check the CRS


st_set_crs(x, crs)
Assign a CRS label without changing coordinates


st_transform(x, crs)
Convert coordinates to another CRS


st_buffer(x, dist)
Create a buffer


st_intersects(x, y)
Test whether geometries share any location


st_touches(x, y)
Test whether geometries touch without interior overlap


st_within(x, y)
Test whether x lies within y


st_filter(x, y)
Keep features based on a spatial relationship


st_union(x)
Merge geometries and dissolve internal boundaries


st_join(x, y)
Join attributes based on spatial relationships


st_distance(x, y)
Calculate distances between geometries

Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

  st_buffer(dist = 0.5) %>%

Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%

title: Week 5: Machine Learning & Linear Regression
text:
Key Concepts

1. Goal of Machine Learning

In this class, ML is used mainly for prediction: producing accurate predictions on new data.
This differs from inference in traditional statistics, which focuses on understanding and explaining relationships between variables.



2. Basic Model Form
\[y = f(x) + \epsilon\] - \(f(x)\): the systematic relationship between \(X\) and \(y\). The model’s job is to estimate \(\hat{f}\). - \(\epsilon\): random error with mean 0. This is the irreducible error. - Prediction error = reducible error (from imperfect estimation of \(f\)) + irreducible error (\(\epsilon\)).


3. Model Flexibility Spectrum: Rigid → Flexible
Linear → Lasso / Ridge → Logistic → Tree-based → Boosting → Neural Network









Direction
Flexibility
Interpretability
Risk




Left (rigid)
Low
High
Underfitting (high bias)


Right (flexible)
High
Low (black box)
Overfitting (high variance)




Lasso (L1): shrinks some coefficients exactly to 0, so it performs variable selection.
Ridge (L2): shrinks all coefficients toward 0 without setting any to 0. Useful when predictors are collinear.
Logistic: used for binary classification. It outputs probabilities.



4. Parametric vs. Non-parametric

Parametric models assume a functional form for \(f\) (e.g., linear) and then estimate its parameters. They are simple, interpretable, and need less data, but they have high bias if the assumed form is wrong.
Non-parametric models assume no fixed form for \(f\) (e.g., trees, KNN). They are highly flexible but need more data and are prone to overfitting.



5. Linear Regression
\[\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p\] - \(\beta_0\): the intercept. - \(\beta_1\): the average change in \(y\) for a one-unit increase in \(x_1\), holding other variables constant. It gives the direction and size of \(x_1\)’s influence.

Least Squares (OLS)

Coefficients are estimated by minimizing the residual sum of squares (RSS): \[\min_{\beta} \; RSS = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\]




6. Evaluation Metrics

\(R^2\): the proportion of variance in \(y\) explained by the model. It ranges from 0 to 1, and higher is better. \[R^2 = 1 - \frac{RSS}{TSS}\]

Note: \(R^2\) always increases when you add variables, so also check Adjusted \(R^2\) or out-of-sample performance.

RMSE: the typical size of prediction errors, in the same units as \(y\). Lower is better. \[RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}\]

For prediction tasks, focus on test-set or CV RMSE.




7. Cross Validation (CV)

Purpose: estimate how the model performs on unseen data, compare models, and tune parameters.
K-Fold CV:

Randomly split the data into K folds.
Train on K−1 folds and validate on the remaining fold.
Repeat K times and average the error (e.g., mean RMSE).

The exercises use K = 10. K = 5 or 10 is a common balance between bias and variance.



8. Over-fitting

An overfit model learns the noise in the training data, so training error is low but test error is high.
More flexible models overfit more easily. This is the bias–variance trade-off.
Remedies: select models with CV, use regularization (Lasso/Ridge), reduce the number of variables, or get more data.



9. Multicollinearity

Multicollinearity means the predictors are highly correlated with each other.
Consequences: unstable coefficient estimates, inflated standard errors, and coefficient signs or magnitudes that are hard to interpret. Prediction accuracy is usually less affected.
Diagnosis: check the correlation matrix or VIF (above 5 or 10 is considered severe).
Remedies: drop or combine variables, use Ridge, or apply PCA.



10. Homoscedasticity

Given all predictors \(X\), the variance of the error term is constant: \[\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_i \mid X) = \sigma^2 \quad (\text{constant})\]
When this fails, the errors are heteroscedastic. Standard errors become biased, so significance tests are unreliable.
Diagnosis: plot residuals vs. fitted values (a funnel shape signals heteroscedasticity), or run the Breusch–Pagan test.
Remedies: log-transform \(y\), use robust standard errors, or use weighted least squares (WLS).

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {

Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}

A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.

  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)

Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.

Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.

text:
Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.
Read one coefficient twice. Choose a variable in your final model. Give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
What’s still missing? Look at your final residual map. Name one thing about those places you’d want to measure next, and where you might get the data.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

Your answer: Among the spatial features, distance to the nearest High Speed station (the SPETA metro station) helped most, reducing CV RMSE from 12.38 to 10.60 percentage points; it may capture transit access that the ACS predictors miss. Regional Rail distance lowers RMSE by only about 0.03 points. Its information may overlap with other predictors. Adding a squared High Speed distance term further improved prediction, yielding a final RMSE of 9.53, about 23% below the baseline. Log-transforming bike density, by contrast, worsened performance.
The income coefficient (\(\hat{\beta} = -1.73\)) indicates that, holding other predictors constant, a $10,000 increase in tract median household income is associated with a 1.73-percentage-point decrease in the share of households without a vehicle. For example, a tract with a median income of $60,000 is predicted to have a zero-vehicle share 1.73 points lower than an otherwise identical tract at $50,000.
The final residual map shows less overprediction in Northeast Philadelphia, but underprediction persists in parts of North Philadelphia and is more apparent in some northwestern tracts. As a next step, I would measure bus service frequency, since rail proximity misses another potentially important transit option. Archived SEPTA GTFS schedules, if available, could provide weekday departure counts.
The uncertainty plot shows no consistent increase in absolute residuals as ACS coefficients of variation rise. Several of the largest errors occur among relatively reliable estimates, and observations with very high CVs are sparse. Sampling uncertainty may contribute to the remaining error, but the plot cannot quantify its share. The persistent spatial patterns also suggest that omitted neighborhood characteristics warrant further investigation.

Rent plus or minus 35% * 1.645 = 58% of med_rentE is the range of uncertainty. If the model’s residual is within that range, it could be just noise.
Flagging tracts with high residuals would tend to flag the least reliable estimates, so we should screen by CV or only flag tracts where the residual exceeds the MOE.

text:
Part 6: Fit vs. prediction






WarningTwo different CVs



Week 3 CV = coefficient of variation: how noisy is one estimate? Today’s CV = cross-validation: how well does a model predict data it hasn’t seen? Same letters, unrelated ideas.



6A: One train/test split

set.seed(5080)
n <- nrow(tracts)
train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = 0.8 * n)

train_data <- tracts[train_idx, ]
test_data  <- tracts[-train_idx, ]

m2_train <- lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = train_data)

test_pred <- predict(m2_train, newdata = test_data)

rmse_train <- sqrt(mean(residuals(m2_train)^2))
rmse_test  <- sqrt(mean((test_data$med_rentE - test_pred)^2))

c(train = rmse_train, test = rmse_test)

   train     test 
260.5748 278.6765 


Stop and look: Which RMSE is larger? Why would you expect that? In words: “The model’s typical miss on tracts it hasn’t seen is about $18 per month.”
Change the seed to any other number and rerun the chunk. Did the test RMSE change? That’s why one split isn’t enough.


6B: 10-fold cross-validation
caret wants a plain data frame, so drop the geometry first. (The geometry isn’t a predictor, and train() will choke on it.)

model_df <- tracts %>% st_drop_geometry()

title: Week 5 In-Class Lab: Where the Model Is Wrong
text:
Part 8: The Challenge
Your team’s job: build the best model for predicting tract median rent, then use it to answer the agency’s question.

Rules

The grade is 10-fold CV RMSE. Use model_df (or tracts) and run set.seed(5080) directly before train(), exactly as in Part 6B, so every team is tested on the same folds.
Don’t drop rows. If you add a variable with missing values, you change the folds and the comparison stops being fair. Fill the gaps or choose a different variable.
You may add any ACS variables (use load_variables(2023, "acs5") to browse) and any spatial feature you can build with Week 4 tools: distances, buffers, counts.
You may not use anything built from rent itself. That rules out med_rentM, rent_cv, rent burden (B25071), and the rent distribution tables (B25063). Ask yourself: would the agency have this variable for a tract whose rent it’s trying to predict? If not, using it is cheating the test. That’s called leakage.



Deliver

Your CV RMSE, in dollars, written as a sentence.
One feature you added, and why. What did you think it would capture that the census variables miss? Did it help?
One coefficient, read twice. Pick a variable in your final model and give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
The agency’s list. Using your final model fit to all tracts, find the five tracts with the largest positive residuals (rent well above expectation). For each, report the residual and the rent CV. Which of the five would you tell the agency to trust, and which might be fog?
Your residual map. Did your added features make the clusters from Part 7B shrink?
